query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermomechanical processing (specifically, controlled cold rolling with a moderate thickness reduction followed by low‐temperature annealing) of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will refine and optimize its duplex lamellar microstructure to simultaneously boost strength, ductility, and resistance to long-term creep and corrosion under extreme service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar eutectic (fcc/B2) structure as produced via casting without post-processing.
generation.intervention: Apply a single step of thermomechanical processing that includes a controlled cold rolling (for example, an 8% reduction, as indicated in prior work) followed by a low-temperature anneal to adjust the lamellar spacing and phase distribution.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed under ambient conditions in the lab with subsequent testing under operational conditions representative of fasteners subjected to extreme temperature fluctuations (room temperature up to ~700°C), long-term mechanical loading including room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined duplex lamellar microstructure with optimized fcc/B2 phase spacing that enhances interphase boundary density.
generation.mechanism: Thermomechanical processing reduces lamellar spacing, which increases the density of phase boundaries that act as barriers to dislocation motion and crack propagation. This two-hierarchical constraint effect enhances strain hardening and promotes microcrack arrest, resulting in improved strength, ductility, and resistance to creep and corrosion—particularly important under fluctuating temperatures and mechanical loads.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast alloy, the treated alloy is expected to show increased tensile and yield strengths, retained or improved ductility, enhanced room-temperature creep resistance, and greater corrosion resistance due to a more uniform microstructure and enhanced protective oxide formation.
generation.baseline: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with its original fine lamellar microstructure, which exhibits insufficient strength and plasticity for demanding industrial fastener applications.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are applicable within the thermal range from ambient to about 700°C, under long-term static and dynamic mechanical loading, and environments where corrosive agents are present. The effect may vary if processing conditions (reduction percentage, annealing temperature/time) deviate significantly from the optimized parameters.
generation.uncertainty: While literature supports strength–ductility enhancement through such thermomechanical treatment, the exact magnitude of improvement in creep and corrosion resistance under fastener-specific extreme conditions is less established and requires detailed investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: one set as the control (as-cast state) and one set processed by the designated thermomechanical treatment (8% cold rolling reduction followed by low-temperature annealing). Conduct comparative tests including room-temperature and elevated temperature tensile tests, long-term creep experiments at room temperature, and accelerated corrosion tests in a simulated service environment. Ensure sufficient sample sizes and repeatability.
measurements: Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to fracture
Creep strain rates over specified time intervals
Corrosion rates and passivation behavior via electrochemical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically processed samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements (e.g., higher strength by a measurable margin, maintained or enhanced ductility, reduced creep strain rate, and lower corrosion rates) relative to the as-cast control group under all test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: These results showed that the yield strength (1437 ± 26 MPa), tensile strength (1562 ± 33 MPa), and elongation (14 ± 1%) of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy after annealing at low temperature were significantly improved compared with the as-cast alloy. Eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit an excellent balance of toughness and strength at room temperature. However, there is still an immediate requirement to design structural components with more strength and ductility due to the increasing technical requirements and harsher operating environments in industrial applications. The demand for stronger and more ductile structural elements has increased as airplane components have become more demanding and technical standards have advanced. Therefore, it is of significance to develop a new eutectic high-entropy alloy with superior properties based on AlCoCrFeNi2.1.

The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5).
